cards.back: First post in the incident channel within 3 minutes at p95, and under $0.50 per investigation.
Root cause accuracy: over 70% at @1 and over 90% at @3. Tool calls, cost and speed are health metrics, not correctness.
Fingerprint each alert by service, symptom and environment, and group matching alerts within a window (say 10 minutes) into one incident with one investigation.
Logs, metrics, deploys, traces and runbooks are queried in parallel with timeouts, so one slow search cannot miss the 3-minute target.
The next query depends on what the last one showed. A step limit and time budget keep it bounded.
Code checks each claim cites a query ID that actually ran, that the result supports it, and that support clears a bar. Below the bar it posts 'low confidence'.
Allow-listed fixes (restart, roll back, scale out), one-click approval in Slack, run through the normal deploy system with a narrow account, then a monitor on the error rate.
About 300 past incidents from postmortems, replayed against a snapshot of that time's data and labelled with the postmortem's root cause.
Two weeks in shadow mode, posting privately to on-call engineers who rate each post, meeting the offline targets before posting publicly.
Thumbs-up below 60% for a week, or any suggested fix that makes an incident worse, sends the assistant back to read-only.

cards.front: Main way the budget gets blown
cards.back: Raw log lines. Summarise log samples in code into top signatures and counts before they reach the model.

quiz.q: During an outage, 200 alerts fire in a minute and the bill spikes with 200 investigations. What was skipped?
choices: Dedup in code: fingerprint and group alerts into one incident before any model call
quiz.why: Alerts with the same fingerprint within a window join one incident and one investigation, with no model call.

quiz.q: p95 time to first post is 5 minutes. Traces show one log search sometimes takes 4 minutes. What do you check first?
choices: That queries run in parallel with per-query timeouts
Whether dedup windows are too long
quiz.why: Parallel queries with timeouts stop one slow search holding up the post.

quiz.q: A post claims 'deploy 4812 caused the spike' citing a query ID that never ran. What should happen?
choices: Post it with a lower confidence score
The evidence gate rejects the claim because the ID is not in the query log
quiz.why: The gate looks up each cited query ID in the investigation's own log; an ID that never ran rejects the claim.

quiz.q: Cost per investigation is $1.20 against $0.50. Most input tokens are raw log lines. What is the fix?
choices: Summarise logs in code into top signatures and counts before the model sees them
quiz.why: Raw log lines are the main way the budget gets blown.

quiz.q: A team proposes 'fixes run ÷ fixes suggested' as the key metric. Why is it misleading?
choices: It rewards pushing fixes, so the system learns to suggest rollbacks too often
It is too hard to compute
quiz.why: Use fix-reverted rate and incidents made worse next to acceptance instead.

quiz.q: An approved rollback runs, but the error rate does not recover after a few minutes. What does the design do?
choices: Say so in the channel, revert the action if safe, and escalate
Close the incident; the fix was approved
quiz.why: The post-fix monitor reports, reverts when safe and escalates.

quiz.q: The logging backend is down during an incident. How should the post handle it?
choices: Infer what the logs probably said
Delay the post until logs return
Say which sources were unavailable and never fill the gaps with guesses
Skip the evidence gate this once
quiz.why: A telemetry outage is a listed risk; the mitigation is to name missing sources, not guess.

quiz.q: Offline accuracy@1 is 74%. Can it post in the public incident channel now?
choices: Not yet: it first runs two weeks in shadow mode and must meet the targets on live incidents
quiz.why: The ship gate is two weeks in shadow mode with ratings before public posts.
